{{distinguish|Hadamard's inequality}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Hermite–Hadamard inequality''', named after [[Charles Hermite]] and [[Jacques Hadamard]] and sometimes also called '''Hadamard's inequality''', states that if a function ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[''a'',&nbsp;''b'']&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is [[convex function|convex]], then the following chain of inequalities hold:

: <math> f\left( \frac{a+b}{2}\right) \le \frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \le \frac{f(a) + f(b)}{2}. </math>

The inequality has been generalized to higher dimensions: if <math> \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n </math> is a bounded, convex domain and <math>f:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> is a positive convex function, then

: <math> \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \int_\Omega f(x) \, dx \leq \frac{c_n}{|\partial \Omega|} \int_{\partial \Omega} f(y) \, d\sigma(y) </math>

where <math> c_n </math> is a constant depending only on the dimension. The best known bound on <math> c_n </math> is <math> c_n \leq 2n^{3/2} </math> and <math> c_n \geq n-1 </math> <ref name=Beck2021 />.
